system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-03-28 14:09:00 to 2184-03-31 21:12:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A female patient with end-stage renal disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, and a history of recurrent hyperkalemia was admitted for weakness, dizziness, and paresthesias. She had recently started baclofen for muscle spasms and took two 10mg doses before experiencing prolonged sleep and new neurological symptoms. In the emergency department, her potassium was 6.7 mEq/L (non-hemolyzed), prompting treatment with calcium gluconate and urgent hemodialysis. Her symptoms were attributed to both hyperkalemia and the sedative effects of baclofen combined with Dilaudid. She underwent multiple dialysis sessions, with potassium normalizing to 4.8 mEq/L. A right heart catheterization revealed improved pulmonary pressures, leading to an increase in her dry weight goal by 2kg to prevent excessive fluid removal. An ultrasound of the left leg showed no deep vein thrombosis despite tenderness. Due to persistent dizziness and safety concerns at home, she was discharged to an extended care rehabilitation facility with follow-up planned with neurology and instructions to monitor weight and INR.
problems: Adverse effect of antiparkinsonism drugs and other central muscle-tone depressants

On ___, Ms. ___ was admitted to the gynecology service 
for treatment of R vulvar cellulitis after an office I&D of 
vulvar sebaceous cysts c/b cellulitis, failing outpatient 
management with Bactrim. 

*) Vulvar Cellulitis 
Upon admission, she was afebrile, VSS. She had no leukocytosis 
or bandemia. Her exam was notable for significant erythema, 
tenderness, and induration along the R vulva, no fluctuance was 
palpated. Given her h/o VRE and complex past medical history, 
infectious disease was consulted who recommended initiating 
vancomycin and unasyn. Pt tolerated both antibiotics well. 

On HD#2, upon clarifying her penicillin allergy (itchy rash), pt 
was transitioned to vancomycin and levaquin, with plan to screen 
for MRSA (nasal and rectal) and discontinue vancomycin if 
negative (results pending at the time of discharge). In 
addition, although erythema improved, repeat exam was notable 
for possible fluctuance. An ultrasound was performed which did 
not show evidence of an underlying drainable abscess. 

On HD#3, her exam was improved with no erythema and decreased 
induration and improved pain. She continued to be afebrile with 
no leukocytosis. 

*) ESRD/HTN 
Renal was consulted to continue pt's hemodialysis while 
inpatient and to assist with ABX dosing. Pt underwent scheduled 
dialysis on HD#1 and HD#3. Pt was continued on sevelamer and 
calcitriol. Her admission Cr was elevated to 7.6 and she was 
hyperkalemic to 5.6 which improved after hemodialysis to 3.1 and 
3.7, respectively on HD#2. 

*) Thrombotic microangiopathy/History of LUE DVT - Her admission 
INR was 1.0. Coumadin had previously been held when pt had 
undergone office I&D procedure. Coumadin was restarted on HD#2 
given no drainable vulvar abscess seen on ultrasound. INR was 
rechecked on HD#3 and noted to be 1.1.

*) Chronic pain - pt was continued on home dose of dilaudid as 
well as lidocaine patches with pain well controlled.
*) Pulmonary HTN - pt was continued on macitentan and sildenafil
*) Seizure disorder - pt was continued on lamotrigine without 
any seizure activity during this admission
*) Migraine headaches - pt was continued on fioricet and 
meclizine as needed.
*) GERD - pt was continued on omeprazole and ranitidine. 
*) OSA - pt was continued on CPAP 

By HD4, her vulva exam was significantly improved with no 
erythema, minimal induration, and decreased tenderness. She was 
tolerating a regular diet, voiding spontaneously, ambulating 
independently, and pain was controlled with oral medications. 
She was then discharged home in stable condition with outpatient 
follow-up scheduled, and plan to continue vancomycin and 
levaquin for 14 days total, with plan to discontinue vancomycin 
if MRSA screens return negative.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your doctors during this stay. You're here because of swelling and redness on your right vulva that started after a cyst drainage in the office. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. It’s been really sore and tender. I thought it would get better after the procedure, but it just kept getting worse. No fever, but the area is hot and hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on Bactrim already, but it didn’t help. We’re treating this as cellulitis—skin infection. Given your medical history, we want to use strong antibiotics to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I remember I had a rash with penicillin before. Is that going to be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good you mentioned that. You’re getting vancomycin and Unasyn for now. Unasyn has penicillin, but since your allergy was just a rash, not severe, we can use it under monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about that. What about my other meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed them all. You’ll keep your Dilaudid for pain, lamotrigine for seizures, warfarin, and your dialysis meds. We’re adjusting doses based on your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had dialysis since yesterday morning. Should I be scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, renal team is on it. You’ll have dialysis today. Your creatinine is high—7.6—and potassium is 5.6, which is concerning. Dialysis will help bring those down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, like last time. I remember high potassium can be dangerous. Will I feel better after dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with the potassium. You’re not having heart symptoms now, which is good. We’ll monitor closely during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative, which is reassuring—no bacteria in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? So it’s just local?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That means the infection hasn’t spread. We’ll keep watching your white count and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re switching your antibiotic. Since your penicillin allergy is mild, we’re stopping Unasyn and starting Levaquin with vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Levaquin covers a broader range and avoids penicillin entirely. Also, we’re checking for MRSA with nasal and rectal swabs. If negative, we can stop vancomycin later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. The redness seems a little less today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But on exam, there was a spot that felt a bit fluid-filled. We’re ordering an ultrasound to make sure there’s no abscess forming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. Good news—no abscess. Just inflammation and a small cyst. No need for another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. I was worried they’d have to cut again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, antibiotics and your body are handling it. We also restarted your warfarin today. It was held before the procedure, but now it’s safe to resume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My INR was low when I came in, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 1.0. We’ll check it again tomorrow. You have antiphospholipid syndrome, so staying on warfarin is important to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ve had DVT before. I don’t want that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your MRSA screens came back negative. That’s great—we can plan to stop vancomycin soon and just continue Levaquin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need the IV antibiotic anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Levaquin is oral, so you can take it at home. You’ll finish a 14-day course total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis? I had it yesterday, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had it yesterday. Your potassium dropped to 3.7 and creatinine to 3.1—much better. We’ll hold off until your next scheduled session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel less tired today. Is my anemia still an issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable around 9.2. It’s low, but not worsening. We’re continuing sevelamer and calcitriol for your bone and mineral balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain is much better with the Dilaudid and patches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep it as needed. Also, your INR is now 1.1—still a bit low, but improving since restarting warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve done really well. The redness is gone, tenderness is minimal. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish all antibiotics—Levaquin every 48 hours for the full course. Take your regular meds, including warfarin, lamotrigine, and dialysis meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis? When’s my next session?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as usual. Just monitor your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for with the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—fever over 100.4, increased redness or drainage, or if pain comes back. Also, watch for trouble urinating or severe belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin? Should I check my INR soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your doctor to monitor INR. It’s still a bit low, but should rise with continued dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on so many meds. Is there a list I can take home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get a full list. Most are the same, just added Levaquin and stopped vancomycin. We also included stool softeners for the Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. I was really worried this might need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. The ultrasound helped us avoid that. Just keep up with follow-up and meds, and you should do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Can I walk stairs at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re walking fine here. No restrictions. Just take it easy the first few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you so much, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The discharge team will give you instructions and prescriptions. Feel better!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any new symptoms? Fever, pain, dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all good. I’ve eaten, used the bathroom, and walked around. Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember—call if anything changes. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with end-stage renal disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, and a history of chronic pain and seizure disorder was admitted for right vulvar cellulitis following an office incision and drainage of sebaceous cysts that failed outpatient treatment with Bactrim. She was afebrile and hemodynamically stable, with no leukocytosis. Treatment was initiated with vancomycin and Unasyn, later transitioned to vancomycin and levaquin after clarification of a mild penicillin allergy. MRSA screens were negative, supporting de-escalation of therapy. An ultrasound showed no abscess, only cellulitis and a right vulvar cyst, avoiding further intervention. She underwent hemodialysis on hospital days 1 and 3, with improvement in creatinine and potassium. Warfarin was restarted on day 2 after ultrasound confirmed no abscess, with INR rising from 1.0 to 1.1. By day 4, her infection had significantly improved, she was ambulating independently, and was discharged home on oral levaquin and her baseline medications with follow-up instructions.
problems: Hypertensive chronic kidney disease with stage 5 chronic kidney disease or end stage renal disease
Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus
Surgical operation with transplant of whole organ as the cause of abnormal reaction of the patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at the time of the procedure
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
